office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Franklin County Community School Corporation (FCCSC) is based in Brookville and runs five schools: Brookville, Laurel and Mt. Carmel (Cedar Grove) elementary schools, Franklin County Middle School and Franklin County High School [24]. State enrollment counts were 1,987 students in 2023-24, 1,944 in 2024-25 and 1,890 in 2025-26 [25]. Dustin Gehring is superintendent and Shannon New is assistant superintendent [26, 27]. Tammy Chavis was superintendent in January 2023 [28]; this guide did not find when the change took place.

The board has seven members [29]. The county's list of officials shows four district seats (Districts 1-4, terms ending in 2028) and three at-large seats held by Kevin Kaiser, Beth Foster and Brandy Wilson, terms ending Dec. 31, 2026 [30]. In 2022, nine candidates ran for the three at-large seats; incumbent Foster and newcomers Kaiser and Wilson won [31, 32]. Officers for 2026: Jessica Brennan (president), Kim Simonson (vice president), Brandy Wilson (secretary) and Kevin Kaiser (legislative liaison) [27].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: the three at-large seats. The state list says 'vote for 1', but the county's 2026 sample ballot says 'Vote for not more than Three (3)' and lists five candidates, all filed as Republicans: Jeffery G Dorrel, Sara Duffy, Kevin Kaiser, Derrike Kolb and Brandy Renae Wilson [6, 33]. Incumbents Kaiser and Wilson are running again; Beth Foster is not on the ballot, so at least one at-large seat will go to a new member [33, 30]. The sample ballot notes that a straight-party vote does not count for this office [33].

Vacancy: District 3 member Kati Holman left the board in September 2026; the board asked District 3 residents to apply by Sept. 25 and scheduled interviews and an appointment for an Oct. 13 special meeting [34, 35]. That seat is not on the 2026 ballot [30].

Enrollment and staffing (April 2026): four elementary teaching positions at Brookville, Laurel and Mount Carmel were to be eliminated at the end of 2025-26, with a drop in enrollment given as the main reason [36]. FCHS principal Michelle South resigned as principal effective June 30, 2026 and stayed on as a teacher [37]; on July 6 the board approved Nicholas Messer as FCHS principal and Matthew Piening as Brookville Elementary principal, both 7-0 [38].

Budget: the advertised 2027 budget totals $35,175,820 (Education Fund $18.0 million, Operations Fund $9.1 million, Debt Service $7,075,820, Rainy Day $1.0 million), with a hearing on Sept. 14, 2026 [39]. The district reported an Education Fund balance of $4,974,088 on June 30, 2026, down from $6,729,847 a year earlier, and an Operations Fund balance of $2,556,648, up from $2,159,877 [40]. Employees got 4% raises for 2025-26, approved in phases in summer 2025 [41]. A public pre-bargaining hearing with the teachers' union was held Sept. 24, 2026 [42]. This guide found no reporting on how the 2025 property-tax law SEA 1 affects FCCSC, and no FCCSC referendum on the 2026 ballot.

Facilities: on July 13, 2026 the board held a first 'preliminary determination' hearing on a project's educational need, cost and tax impact [40]. At the July 6 special meeting it discussed bond details and building projects [38]. On July 13 it voted 4-3 to buy 0.547 acres at Wildcat Lane and State Road 101 for $75,000 (Kaiser, Wilson, Holman and Brennan yes; Simonson, Burris and Foster no) [40]. A district committee began work in September 2026 on a '2026 Unified Progressive Design-Build Project', including a request for qualifications [43].

Board votes: several 2026 votes split the board. Beth Foster was elected Board of Finance president 5-2 and Kim Simonson vice president 5-2, with Wilson and Kaiser voting no both times [27]. In August 2026 the board voted 5-2 on Kaiser's motion to seek competitive bids for employee insurance coverage before bargaining; Foster and Simonson voted no [44].

Safety and discipline: FCCSC received an $86,000 state Secured School Safety grant in 2026 [45]. In August 2026 it began an out-of-school suspension program with Franklin County Court Services and Stayin' Alive, where suspended students do schoolwork and prevention programming [46].
Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum, questionnaire or news profile for this race, and no campaign websites.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, elected in 2022; past board president and current legislative liaison [47, 27].
background: Won an at-large seat in November 2022 and was sworn in in January 2023 [32, 28].

According to WRBI, he was president of the Board of Finance for two years, was elected board president in his third year, and is in his fourth year as legislative liaison [47]. He was re-elected legislative liaison 7-0 in January 2026 [27].
Received the Indiana School Boards Association's Level 4 Exemplary Governance Award for 2025, its highest individual award for board training, with 255 professional development points [47].
path_to_ballot: Appears on the 2026 ballot as a Republican [6, 33].

items: On board training, he said 'serving on the school board comes with a responsibility to be informed and engaged' and that 'professional development isn't just a requirement—it's part of doing the job well and making decisions that are in the best interest of students and the community.' [47]
In August 2026 he moved that the board have administrators seek competitive bids for the district's insurance coverage before bargaining started; the motion passed 5-2 [44].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member. In 2026 he voted against Beth Foster as Board of Finance president and Kim Simonson as vice president (both passed 5-2) [27]. He made the motion for the 0.547-acre land purchase on Wildcat Lane, which passed 4-3 [40].
